messages.subject: reading timezone and start time
parts:
Hi,

Thank you for this excellent software! I'm new to the GGIR package, but have read through the tutorial, package documentation, and have searched the archives on this group. I am working with cwa data collected with AX3 axivity units and have 2 basic questions:

1) When using g.shell.GGIR(), the vignette tells me that "strategy" in combination with "hrs.del.start" and "hrs.del.end" can be used to subset incoming data by removing a certain number of hours from the beginning and end of the total file (the documentation describes it as how many hours after start of the experiment did wearing of the monitor start). In my experiment, however, I simply started the units some time in advance and noted the time at which wearing began. So in order to calculate the number of hours, I would have to extract the start time from the unit, calculate the number of hours between that time and when wearing started, and then enter that value here from processing. This can be done, but I feel like I must be missing an easier option to simply state the actual timestamp at which wearing started. Is this possible?

2) The first issue caused me to look into the function g.cwaread(), which I believe works under the hood for g.shell.GGIR. In this case, I can directly specify a start and end time point for reading data in "year-month-day hr:min:sec" format. This works, but I am having trouble understanding the function of the "desiredtz" argument in g.cwaread(). My data were collected in the UTC+08 timezone, and thus I do the following:

ac1 <- g.cwaread(fileName = "myfile.cwa", 
          start = as.POSIXct("2020/03/02 17:00:00", tz= "Asia/Kuala_Lumpur"), 
          end = as.POSIXct("2020/03/05 08:20:00", tz="Asia/Kuala_Lumpur"))

However, I am surprised to see that this gives me a different output than if I specify desiredtz directly:

ac2 <- g.cwaread(fileName = "myfile.cwa", 
          start = as.POSIXct("2020/03/02 17:00:00", tz= "Asia/Kuala_Lumpur"), 
          end = as.POSIXct("2020/03/05 08:20:00", tz="Asia/Kuala_Lumpur"), desiredtz = "Asia/Kuala_Lumpur")

I originally assumed that these would give me the same output because the devices were synced to this same timezone when they were configured and collected data. So it is unclear to me what exactly that argument is doing. The package documentation says to see g.getmeta() for details on this argument, but that only gives a link to a webpage with timezones. Could anyone comment on which of the above two approaches is appropriate?

Thank you!

Tom Kraft
Postdoc
UC Santa Barbara

Hello Vincent,

Thank you for the help and reply. Unfortunately as a postdoc I don't have any funding that could be put towards this cause, so I will likely be stuck with workarounds for now. But I do have two ideas:

1) The function g.cwaread() is already designed to subset data based on a datetime (ymd hms) for beginning and end of data collection. Because g.shell.GGIR() is internally calling g.cwaread() (based on looking into the source code on github), it seems like it might be straightforward to implement a strategy 4 that only works for this filetype but utilizes the already built in arguments "start" and "end". I tried to figure out how to implement this but I can't seem to figure out where internal arguments are passed to g.cwaread(). In either case though, it doesn't appear that this would require additional functionality?

2) An alternative approach would be if I could load data with g.cwaread(), which currently works fine, and then feed that object into g.shell.GGIR. It seems like this should be possible but I can't figure out how to do this. I'm not used to working with hierarchical functions that do things like load and analyze data all in one step, so it's possible that I'm missing an obvious way to feed in data that has already been loaded into the environment.

Is there a chance that one of these approaches would offer a very quick solution? Thank you!

Tom

messages.author: 13568954e9b4ef4b
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: reading timezone and start time
parts:
I think the quickest work around is to process the data with GGIR part 1 as you would normally do. Next, you will have to write an R script that does the following:
- Load the milestone (RData) files generated by GGIR part 1 as stored in the meta/basic folder.
- Create an extra timestamp column in object M$metalong by converting the timestamps to POSIX value with GGIR function iso8601chartime2POSIX.
- Change the non-wear score column in object M$metalong to 3 for all values outside your time interval of interest.
- Save all object you found in the milestone file back to the same file, including the now modified object M.
- Continue with part 2 with default settings for strategy. All time outside your value of interest will be treated as accelerometer non-wear time.

The other approaches you suggest are not going to work I think.

Good luck, Vincent

Hi Vincent,

The custom code that I generated based on this thread has worked well, but I see that at some point you implemented the "study_dates_file" parameter. Could you simply verify that when used with a csv file denoting the start and end dates of expected wear, that the end result will only reflect data collected within this window (based on the masking parameters set in tandem), thus accomplishing the goals laid out earlier in this thread?

I see here (https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/4e33a636599759e438f36fa0c76ace0165d71235/R/g.impute.R#L99) that the function is called within g.impute(), but could you also quickly comment on which part of GGIR this will run in? parts:
Hi Tom,

The study_dates_file parameter was indeed recently added, and is one of the ways GGIR part 2 allows for specifying what time segment(s) of the recording it should ignore (mask) from further analysis. Other arguments such as hrs.del.start are used on top of this and will apply relative to the dates window as specified.

As a result, part 1 will not be affected and will always read and pre-process the entire recording. I am aware that computationally this is not efficient for recordings with a lot of time to be masked. However, I implemented it in the current way because:
  • Most studies I have worked with do not have this problem as their sensors are typically worn from the first till the last recording day.
  • Processing all data in a file offers a complete overview of the recording and ensures no data is skipped that could have been used.
However, if you think it could help to have a GGIR option to only read and process the expected time window then that is technically possible to build. However, I would then need funding for my time to work on that. If you see opportunities for that then please pm me.

Best wishes,

Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees | Independent consultant | https://accelting.com/
